items.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: I know damn well that there are circumstances... certainly a lot of careers would not have happened in the same way... I'll tell you, knowing what I do about some of the personalities that I dealt with... a perfectly good description of Rollins, of Wes Montgomery, of Bill Evans.

ctx.x: Right. Well I have to congratulate you on the contribution you’ve made to the art form called jazz. It’s really quite amazing the things you’ve been involved in and the careers that you have helped.

Well I must admit that I look back on it with a good deal of satisfaction. I’ve been very fortunate because in this business in particular, a lot of the associations that you form, at least initially, are accidental as hell. If someone tells me that I have been helpful to this or that career that’s exactly the thing that I want to hear because I have always looked on the role of the producer in a very specific way. Now one of the hardest things, and I’ve been at it, I’m getting perilously close to my fiftieth…

with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects…

items.title: Orrin Keepnews — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Cannonball coming into my office one morning... telling me, 'I heard this really great guitar player. We’ve got to get him for the label.' ... It’s Bill Evans and Wes Montgomery that stand out as an art. They are just a matter of my being told about somebody and having followed up on it.

ctx.x: Wes Montgomery. Yes. Actually, I guess when you’re putting things in order; it’s Bill Evans and Wes Montgomery that stand out as an art. They are just a matter of my being told about somebody and having followed up on it. That sequence of events thing that I was starting to talk to you about with the presence of Clark leading to the Adderely’s, and the really the next step in that story is Cannonball coming into my office one morning. He had just gotten back from a one-nighter in Indianapolis and telling me, “I…
Into Riverside, or Prestige? He came to your office?

items.title: Orrin Keepnews — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He recommended and engineer who he said was excellent, and had done an album for him of the…the Master Sounds, Wess’ two brothers.

ctx.x: Orrin, we’re going to loose time talking about your recent achievements in the last couple decade.

No, wait a minute. I know that. I’m going to get this straight first. The starting of me, and the last time I started a label, was Landmark. Okay, Landmark came about because, let me give you a quick chain of command, and I’ll do it quickly. Monk, we know the story of how Monk came into the plan. The first breakthrough record for Monk on Riverside was “Brilliant Cornish.” The final session of that, we had two tunes yet to be done; we finished that. We showed up at the studio, and Monk, without

bothering to tell me about it, had made two changes in the band. One of them was actually there before I got there. The only time we could get, we were working at Reeves, was late morning into early afternoon kind of thing. I think we had like a ten-o-clock start. I get there, and one of the people was already there, but he was fast asleep on the floor on the studio. That was a young bass player, who had recently started working for Miles Davis. Having had a fight with Oscar Pettiford during the previous session.…
